title: What School Leaders Might Take From Carl Hendrick's Instructional Illusions Webinar
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes draws lessons for school leaders from Carl Hendrick's webinar on 'Instructional Illusions,' centring on the gap between performance and learning. She argues that schools too often build systems around the wrong signals, mistaking calm, busy, productive-looking lessons for evidence that anything will be remembered a week later. From this she draws a caution about lesson observation: leaders should ask how many pupils are thinking, and how hard, rather than being impressed by surface features. She then works through Hendrick's points on motivation growing out of success, shared human cognition over bespoke learning routes and learning styles, the tendency to equate novelty with improvement, and the difficulty experts have in making their knowledge visible. Each point is translated into a leadership habit, from engineering the next success for struggling pupils to resisting new initiatives and using coaching to make expert thinking explicit. Her overall move is to urge leaders to become more suspicious of appearances.
points: Hughes argues that busy pupils, tidy books, confident answers and polished routines can all coexist with thin, short-lived learning, so leaders should not treat them as proof of learning.

Because classroom feedback is delayed and unreliable, unlike a tennis ball landing in or out, short lesson visits tell leaders less than they pretend; the better question is how many pupils are thinking and how hard.
Following Hendrick, she reverses the usual order of motivation and achievement: motivation often grows out of success, so the leader's question is where to engineer the next success.
She treats the 'innovation illusion' as a direct warning to leaders, arguing that leadership sometimes means resisting the urge to add another initiative and improving what is already there.
Expert teachers' knowledge is largely automatic, so placing novices near experts is not enough; coaching must make expert thinking visible and break practice into nameable parts.
quotes: Too often in schools, we can end up building systems around the wrong signals. A lesson can appear purposeful, calm and productive. Pupils may be completing work, answering questions and staying on task.

Carl made the point that classrooms are messy places in which feedback is delayed and often unreliable. In a sport like tennis, you know straight away whether the ball landed in or out. In teaching, the result of a decision may not be clear until much later.
For school leaders, that should make us more cautious about observation. A short visit to a lesson can tell us something, but not as much as we sometimes pretend.
When pupils have a history of finding a subject difficult, telling them to be more motivated is not much use. A better question is where we can engineer the next success.

Schools sometimes reach too quickly for highly personalised approaches when what is needed is stronger whole-class teaching, clearer explanation and more careful practice. That is not an argument against support or adaptation. It is simply a reminder that not every difference requires a different method.

That is a hard message for leaders because it cuts against the instinct to be seen to be doing something. Sometimes leadership means introducing a useful change but sometimes it means resisting the urge to add another thing, instead improving the quality of what is already there. That is less glamorous, but often more sensible.

If we want less experienced teachers to improve, it is not enough to place them near expertise and hope they absorb it. We need ways of making expert thinking visible. That is one reason why careful coaching matters.
